description: Five qualitative real-gas isotherms, three coexistence plateaus, dashed envelope and critical K with pressure/volume guides. Complete n38/n39 context; registered modern liquid-left V1/V1-prime and vapor-right V2-prime/V2 correction declared separately from original reversed labels. No numeric readings.

authoritativeText.text:
38. Isotherms of a real gas

Observing evaporation or boiling alone is not enough to understand how a gas becomes a liquid and how a liquid becomes a gas again.
We also need to study how a real gas's pressure and volume change at different temperatures.

The textbook illustrates this process by slowly compressing carbon dioxide under a piston in a cylinder (Figure $54$).
The closed cylinder contains a fixed total mass of a pure substance.
Choose a temperature below its critical temperature, at which liquid and vapor can exist together in equilibrium.

During compression, the surroundings transfer energy to the substance by doing work on it.
Its actual change in internal energy also depends on heat exchanged at the same time.
We cannot say that compression at constant temperature always increases internal energy.

To keep temperature $T$ constant, the cylinder must exchange enough heat with its surroundings.
In the textbook's apparatus, the cylinder is placed in a large container of liquid maintained at a constant temperature.
Compression is slow enough for heat released during compression and condensation to pass to the surroundings.

At a constant temperature, when the gas occupies a large volume and is relatively dilute, reducing its volume raises its pressure approximately according to the Boyle-Mariotte law.
Further compression makes the real gas depart from this approximation.
Once condensation starts, further reduction in volume leaves the pressure constant if temperature and liquid-vapor equilibrium are maintained.

The textbook describes seeing transparent liquid appear through an observation window in the cylinder.
Some of the gaseous substance has condensed into liquid.



Figure 54

Continue slowly compressing the substance at constant temperature while liquid and vapor coexist.
The liquid's mass increases, and the vapor's mass decreases by the same amount.
The closed system's total mass does not change.

The pressure gauge's reading stays constant until all the vapor has condensed and the substance beneath the piston is entirely liquid.
The masses and volumes of the two phases change.
Matter does not appear from nowhere or disappear.

After condensation is complete, even a small further decrease in the liquid's volume causes a large increase in pressure.
A liquid is difficult to compress, but it is not absolutely incompressible.

At constant temperature $T$, a curve showing the relation between pressure $P$ and volume $V$ is called an **isotherm** (Figure 54).
Here, volume means the total volume of the fixed mass of substance in the cylinder.
When liquid and vapor coexist, it includes the volumes occupied by both phases.

Condensation begins at volume $V_2$ and ends at volume $V_1$.
In the illustrated compression at constant temperature, $V\geq V_2$ corresponds to the vapor state.

At equality, the substance is at the saturated-vapor boundary where condensation is just beginning.
For $V<V_1$, it is liquid.

Between the two endpoints, liquid and vapor coexist.
Do not mistake the total volume in this interval for the volume of a fixed mass of vapor alone.

The textbook explains that other substances can have similar isotherms when the temperature is not too high.
This means temperatures below each substance's critical temperature, with states that allow liquid and vapor to coexist in equilibrium.
It does not include every temperature or every state of matter.

On the coexistence part of compression at constant temperature, total volume decreases from $V_2$ to $V_1$.
Pressure stays constant as vapor gradually becomes liquid.

Points on the straight segment $B-A$ of the isotherm correspond to liquid-vapor equilibrium.
The endpoints mark where one phase first appears or finally disappears.

At one equilibrium state with fixed temperature and total volume, the masses of the two phases do not change with time.
At a different equilibrium point, their mass proportions can be different.
Microscopically, molecules keep leaving the liquid surface and returning to the liquid.

At equilibrium, the average numbers leaving and returning in the same time are equal.
The net effects of evaporation and condensation balance.
Equilibrium does not mean that molecules stop moving.

**Vapor in equilibrium with its liquid is called saturated vapor.**
For a fixed temperature, a fixed space occupied by vapor holds a certain mass of vapor in equilibrium with the liquid.
If that same space temporarily contains extra vapor at the same temperature, the extra vapor condenses into liquid until equilibrium returns.

The textbook's statement that there cannot be more vapor describes liquid-vapor equilibrium.
It is not an absolute restriction on a short-lived state that is not in equilibrium.

The vapor pressure $p_0$ when a liquid and its vapor are in equilibrium is called the **saturated vapor pressure**.
For this lesson's pure substance, at fixed temperature and while both phases still coexist, it does not change when the total volume changes.
This conclusion cannot be used without those conditions once coexistence ends or the temperature changes.

Saturated vapor pressure can stay constant because compression causes some vapor to condense.
The same mass occupies much less volume as liquid than as vapor.

Compressing the vapor above the liquid temporarily disturbs equilibrium, slightly increasing vapor density and pressure.
More molecules then return to the liquid than escape from it.

Net condensation follows until equilibrium is restored.
As long as temperature is unchanged and both liquid and vapor remain, the equilibrium vapor density and pressure return to their previous values.

This requires the vapor's mass to decrease through condensation.
It does not mean that compressing a fixed mass of vapor also leaves its pressure unchanged.

Now consider an isotherm for the same mass of carbon dioxide at a higher constant temperature that is still below the critical temperature (Figure 55).
At large volume, where the gas is dilute, it still approximately follows an ideal-gas isotherm.

The prime mark labels the endpoints on this higher-temperature curve.
The horizontal liquid-vapor coexistence segment begins at volume $V_2'<V_2$.

Keep decreasing the volume until condensation is complete.
The liquid-end volume is larger than for the lower-temperature curve:

$V_1'>V_1$.
The isotherm then becomes steep.

At volume $V_1'$, all the substance in the cylinder is liquid.
The endpoint subscripts follow the definitions used earlier.



Figure 55

39. 临界温度

比较实验得到的真实气体等温线（图55），可以看出液汽共存段接近临界点时的变化。
这里比较同一种纯物质、相同总质量在不同恒定温度下的状态，而不是要求所有物质在所有温度下都服从同一条曲线。
温度升高时，开始凝结的蒸汽体积减小，蒸汽密度增大；

凝结完成时的液体体积增大，液体密度减小。
原书用分子运动增强、形成液态需要更高的蒸汽密度来作定性解释。
这不意味着分子被逐个排成静止队列，也不是从这个图像就能算出相变条件。

液体膨胀与两相密度接近，使相应的水平共存段逐渐缩短。
在每个温度下，平衡液体与蒸汽的压强相同；
沿共存条件升温，这两相的密度越来越接近。

不同温度所对应的平衡压强也会改变，不能把这里的比较理解为整个升温过程压强固定。

随着温度接近某个值，等温线的水平共存段越来越短，最后缩为一点。
这个温度叫做临界温度；
能够出现这种液汽临界点的物质各有自己的临界温度。

原书给出的近似值是：二氧化碳（$\mathrm{CO}_2$）为 $t_{\text{临}}\sim31^\circ\mathrm{C}$，水为 $t_{\text{临}}\sim374^\circ\mathrm{C}$。
沿液汽共存条件接近临界点，两相的差别消失，比汽化热趋于零。

原书说临界温度时汽化热等于零，是指这一相变潜热的极限，不是说临界附近加热物质不需要能量，也不是任意温度下的汽化热都为零。

在 $T=T_{\text{临}}$ 的等温线上，原水平共存段缩成的那个点叫做临界态，也叫临界点。
临界点的压强叫做临界压强；
仅仅温度达到临界温度，还不足以确定物质就在临界点。

原书给出二氧化碳的临界压强约为 $7.4\times10^6$ 牛顿/米$^2$（73 大气压），水的近似值为 $p_{\text{临}}=22.0\times10^6$ 牛顿/米$^2$（218 大气压）。
一定质量的物质在临界点有相应的临界体积，这个总体积与物质的总质量有关。

原书所说液体体积最大、饱和汽压强最大，是指固定质量的饱和液体沿本课共存曲线趋近临界点时的端点，以及饱和汽压曲线的临界终点。
它不表示任意液体都有一个与条件无关的最大体积，也不表示物质的压强不能超过临界压强。

把固定质量的物质保持在临界温度并缓慢压缩，密度逐渐增大，经过临界点时达到临界密度。
在临界点，原先平衡液体与蒸汽的密度差消失，不能再把它们区分为两个不同的相。
继续压缩可得到更高密度、具有液体样性质的单相流体，不能把这一段无条件称为“气缸中全部是通常意义的液体”。

这条路径没有低于临界温度时那样的有限液汽共存区间，也没有液体与蒸汽之间的两相界面。
这里的连续转变是相态和密度变化的连续性，不是说临界附近的物性没有显著变化。

原书用透明密闭容器中的物质来说明临界点附近的观察现象（图56a）。
容器内物质的总质量固定，容器体积选为这份物质的临界体积，初始状态有液体与蒸汽共存。
在这一特定条件下缓慢加热，接近临界温度时液汽界面变得不清晰、不稳定（图56b），到达临界点时界面消失（图56c）。

这些是原书实验的示意描述，不是说任何密闭容器一旦加热到临界温度就必然到达临界点。

原书描述反向冷却时，容器中出现浓雾，形成许多小液滴（图56d）。
在回到液汽共存状态的过程中，小液滴逐渐汇合，在通常重力条件下重新出现液体在下、蒸汽在上的界面（图56e）。
可见的雾滴属于液态，不是把蒸汽分子本身看见了；

这里保留的是原书特定实验路径的现象。



图 56

原书将乙醚列为观察这些现象的历史实验材料，理由是它的临界压强相对较低，书中近似值为约36大气压，临界温度为 $194^\circ\mathrm{C}$。
这里仅保留并阅读原书实验的描述与数据，不把“最好用乙醚”作为儿童自行操作的建议，也不提供密闭加热或加压的操作步骤。

原书封2扉页的表列出了由实验测得的一些物质的临界温度。
这是对原书表格位置的引用，不表示本课重新测定或独立校准了那些数值。

在高于临界温度的恒定温度下，从较大体积开始压缩，通常会使压强增大。
只有气体足够稀薄、相互作用影响较小时，才可以近似使用理想气体状态方程；
高温或超临界状态本身并不保证气体是理想气体。

在本课讨论的流体状态范围内，只靠这种等温压缩，不能产生液体与蒸汽分开的两相凝结。
若保持压强不变而降温到临界温度以下，结果还取决于所保持的压强和经过的状态路径。
在低于临界压强、且能经过液汽共存区的路径上，降温可导致凝结并出现液汽界面。

若保持高于临界压强并沿单相路径冷却，物质可以连续变得更稠密、具有液体样性质，而没有突然出现的两相界面。
原书所说“看不到液体的形成过程”应理解为后一类连续路径，不可概括为所有恒压降温都必然凝结却看不到界面。

原书用氯和氧气作比较：氯在室温下可通过适当的等温压缩液化；
氧气要靠压缩产生液汽两相转变，必须先冷却到低于 $-118^\circ\mathrm{C}$ 的温度。
这里保留原书的近似温度数据；

低于临界温度是这种液化的必要条件，还必须配合适当的压强，并不是降到该温度以下就自动全部液化。
这些例子用于说明物质之间的差别，不是气体加压或制冷的操作建议。

inventory.description: One p-V family with origin 0, upward pressure arrow and rightward volume arrow; no numeric ticks or units. Five solid isotherms are visible, labelled T, T1, T2, critical Tk and T3. T, T1 and T2 have three progressively higher and shorter horizontal coexistence plateaus. The critical curve is bold and has a locally horizontal tangent at labelled K; the upper T3 curve has no finite horizontal coexistence plateau. One dashed two-sided coexistence envelope passes through all six subcritical plateau endpoints and K, ending at the volume axis on both sides. A solid horizontal critical-pressure guide runs from the pressure axis to K. Solid volume guides descend to the volume axis from the low-temperature endpoints, middle-temperature endpoints and K. The original bottom labels from left to right are V2, V2-prime, critical Vk, V1-prime, V1. These source families reverse the convention already established in fig54 and n38. The two higher-temperature T2 plateau endpoints are visible on the dashed envelope but have no additional printed bottom volume labels or extra vertical guides. All source curve endpoints are finite and retained; no extrapolated high-pressure branch, new temperature value or added cycle is warranted. Modern additions: Registered modern endpoint notation: source left V2/V2-prime display V1/V1-prime; source right V1-prime/V1 display V2-prime/V2. This is an explicitly declared correction, not claimed source lettering. English c denotes critical in p_c, V_c and T_c; source point K stays K. Source temperature indices T1, T2 and T3 remain indices, not numeric temperature readings. Axis-wise affine drawing scaling and tiered bottom labels retain source volume order without assigning calibrated physical coordinates. The full current n38 and n39 title/prose/captions and n39 shared attachment are bound. Uncertainties: The hand-drawn curves are qualitative and uncalibrated. Internal drawing coordinates and slopes are not supplied thermodynamic data.
